query: For an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy made from low-activation refractory elements, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations expected relative to pure tungsten, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy relative to pure tungsten arise because its microstructure self-organizes into dendritic regions rich in high-melting-point elements (W, Ta) interspersed with softer interdendritic regions enriched in lower melting point elements (Ti, V, Zr). Under high-temperature loading, these softer regions serve as strain‐accommodating channels that promote dislocation motion and delay crack propagation, while the harder dendritic regions maintain overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy produced by vacuum arc melting, exhibiting a multiphase dendritic microstructure with regions of compositional segregation (W/Ta-rich dendrites and Ti/V/Zr-enriched interdendritic phases).
generation.intervention: Subject both the WTaTiVZr HEA and commercially pure tungsten to identical high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compressive loading) under conditions relevant to plasma-facing-component service.
generation.conditions: High-temperature mechanical loading (approximately 1200–1500°C) in an inert atmosphere with controlled strain rates so that thermal activation enables dislocation glide and phase-specific deformation in the alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: Microstructural heterogeneity – specifically, the presence of distinct dendritic and interdendritic regions resulting from elemental segregation.
generation.mechanism: At high temperature, the lower-melting-point, softer interdendritic phases become readily deformable, facilitating dislocation nucleation and motion, which enhances plastic strain. Simultaneously, the hard, W/Ta-enriched dendrites provide solid solution strengthening and inhibit rapid crack propagation, thereby improving toughness compared to pure tungsten, which lacks such heterogeneity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The HEA will exhibit a higher plastic strain (greater ductility) and a greater area under the stress-strain curve (improved toughness) during high-temperature tests, with microstructural observations showing pronounced deformation in the softer interdendritic regions and more distributed damage, as opposed to the more brittle and localized failure observed in pure tungsten.
generation.baseline: Commercially pure tungsten tested under the same high-temperature mechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under service-relevant high temperatures (around 1200–1500°C) and controlled loading rates; deviations in processing that significantly alter the phase distribution or at lower temperatures where thermal activation is limited could cause the effect to diminish or disappear.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in plasticity and toughness, and the relative contribution of other potential high-entropy alloy strengthening mechanisms (such as solid-solution strengthening) is uncertain. Additional characterization is necessary to quantitatively separate the effects of dendritic segregation from other alloying contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the equimolar WTaTiVZr HEA and commercially pure tungsten with similar dimensions and processing histories. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or compressive loading at 1300°C) in an inert atmosphere. Utilize real-time imaging (e.g., high-temperature optical/SEM) and post-test microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EBSD) to assess the deformation behaviors and fracture modes.
measurements: Plastic strain (%) and ductility measures under high-temperature loading
Fracture surface morphology and crack propagation patterns
Microstructural changes in dendritic and interdendritic regions during deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA does not show a statistically significant improvement in plastic strain and toughness compared to pure tungsten, or if detailed microstructural analyses fail to reveal deformation localized within softer interdendritic regions (with no clear role of elemental segregation in enhancing ductility), then the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

In this work, novel high-strength, low-activation Wx(TaVZr)100−x (x = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25) refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) were prepared by vacuum arc melting. Their microstructure, compressive mechanical properties, hardness, and fracture morphology were investigated and analyzed. The results show that the RHEAs possess a disordered BCC phase, ordered Laves phase, and Zr-rich HCP phase. Their dendrite structures were observed, and the distribution of dendrites became gradually more dense with an increase in W content. The RHEAs demonstrate high strength and hardness, with these properties being higher than in most reported tungsten-containing RHEAs. For example, the typical W20(TaVZr)80 RHEA has a yield strength of 1985 MPa and a hardness of 636 HV, respectively. The improvement in terms of strength and hardness are mainly due to solid solution strengthening and the increase in dendritic regions. During compression, with the increase in the applied load, the fracture behavior of RHEAs changed from initial intergranular fractures to a mixed mode combining both intergranular and transgranular fractures.

In this work, novel high-strength, low-activation Wx(TaVZr)100−x RHEAs were designed and prepared. The effect of various W contents on the microstructures and mechanical properties of the RHEAs were explored. The phase formation, strengthening mechanisms, and fracture behavior were also analyzed and discussed. The main findings of the present work are summarized as follows: (1) The prepared RHEAs have three different phases. In addition to the main disordered BCC solid solution phase, Laves and Zr-rich HCP phases were also detected. Through detailed analysis, it was confirmed that the Laves phase is an intermetallic compound (V2Zr) formed by V and Zr elements. (2) With an increase in W content, the microstructure of the RHEAs changed significantly, from a slender dendrite shape to a coarser dendrite shape, and the distribution of dendrites continuously became denser. The W and Ta elements with high melting points were mainly concentrated in dendritic regions, while the V and Zr elements with low melting points were concentrated in interdendritic regions.
